title: The central and peripheral nervous systems
note: The cerebrum's lobes divide labor: frontal for movement and planning, parietal for body sensation, temporal for hearing and memory, occipital for vision. In the spinal cord, posterior (dorsal) means sensory and anterior (ventral) means motor. The autonomic system has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

read.title: Sensory in back, motor in front
text: The spinal cord follows a simple rule: posterior means sensory and anterior means motor. In cross section, its gray matter forms a butterfly or H shape. The posterior horns receive and process incoming sensory signals. The anterior horns hold the large motor neurons whose axons leave the cord to reach skeletal muscles. In the thoracic and upper lumbar cord, and in the sacral cord, small lateral horns hold autonomic neurons.

The spinal nerves obey the same rule. Each nerve joins the cord by two roots. Sensory fibers enter through the posterior root, whose swelling, the dorsal root ganglion, contains the cell bodies of the sensory neurons. Motor fibers leave through the anterior root. The two roots merge into one mixed nerve, so almost every spinal nerve carries both sensory and motor signals.

Around the gray matter lies white matter, organized into columns of myelinated axons. The posterior columns carry ascending sensory tracts to the brain, while the lateral and anterior columns carry a mix of ascending and descending tracts.
The brain repeats the pattern in its own way. In the cerebral cortex, the precentral gyrus is the primary motor area and the postcentral gyrus, just behind it, is the primary area for body sensation.
